claims.title: The first settlers reach the islands
claims.summary: Archaic Ortoiroid peoples migrated from the South American mainland into Trinidad, the earliest of several waves of indigenous settlement that populated the twin islands over millennia.

claims.title: Arawak and Carib peoples established
claims.summary: By the time of European contact the islands were home to Arawakan-speaking groups such as the Nepoya and Suppoya and Cariban speakers such as the Yao, peoples whose roots lay in the Orinoco region.

claims.title: Columbus sights Trinidad and Tobago
claims.summary: On his third voyage Christopher Columbus reached Trinidad, naming it after the Holy Trinity, and sighted Tobago — the first European contact with islands then inhabited by Arawak and Carib peoples.

claims.title: Spain founds San José de Oruña
claims.summary: Antonio de Berrio took possession of Trinidad and founded San José de Oruña (St Joseph), establishing the first effective Spanish settlement on an island the crown had claimed but long neglected.

claims.title: Raleigh raids the Spanish settlement
claims.summary: Sir Walter Raleigh attacked the Spanish settlement while searching for El Dorado, underscoring how weak and exposed the Spanish colony on Trinidad remained.

claims.title: The Cédula de Población
claims.summary: King Charles III's Cédula de Población offered free land and tax breaks to Roman Catholic settlers, drawing French planters with their enslaved Africans and free coloureds and remaking Trinidad as a plantation society.

claims.title: Britain captures Trinidad
claims.summary: A British expedition under Sir Ralph Abercromby took Trinidad from Spain almost without a fight; the last Spanish governor, Chacón, signed the capitulation at the Valsayn estate.

claims.summary: After centuries of being fought over by the Dutch, Courlanders, French, and British, Tobago was finally awarded to Britain by the Treaty of Paris of 1814.

claims.title: Abolition of slavery
claims.summary: Under Britain's Slavery Abolition Act, slavery ended in Trinidad and Tobago on 1 August 1834, though a transitional 'apprenticeship' kept the freed people tied to the estates.

claims.title: Full emancipation
claims.summary: The apprenticeship system ended on 1 August 1838, granting the formerly enslaved full freedom and leaving the colony's planters scrambling for new sources of labour.

claims.summary: The ship Fatel Razack landed the first indentured Indian labourers in Trinidad; over 147,000 Indians would arrive under indenture by 1917, transforming the colony's population and culture.

claims.title: Tobago united with Trinidad
claims.summary: Britain amalgamated Tobago with the wealthier colony of Trinidad to cut administrative costs; in 1899 Tobago became a ward, creating the single colony of Trinidad and Tobago.

claims.summary: An oilbelt strike led by Tubal Uriah 'Buzz' Butler spread into riots across the colony, leaving at least fourteen dead and giving birth to Trinidad and Tobago's modern trade-union and nationalist movements.

claims.summary: Mass marches and protests over racial and economic inequality, with a mutiny in the army, forced Eric Williams to declare a state of emergency in the most serious challenge to his government.

claims.summary: A new constitution replaced the British monarch with a president as head of state; the last governor-general, Sir Ellis Clarke, became the republic's first president.

claims.title: Birth of the steelpan
claims.summary: Musicians in Port of Spain fashioned the steelpan from oil drums after colonial bans on African drumming — the only acoustic instrument invented in the 20th century and now the national instrument.
